memories.memory_text: Alex shoved a 'Just Say Yes' pamphlet into my hand like it was some kind of life raft, grinning like he’d just discovered fire.
I watched Alex start hurling rocks at the bank out of nowhere—completely unhinged—and then get tackled by security, still yelling at me to go to that damn seminar.

I sat there, trying to keep my voice steady when Norman offered me the loan specialist job—52 grand, not just dollars—and I could feel the weight of it, like saying yes to something bigger than I’d planned.

I took the Maniyesto from Sanji, reading through the rules—saying yes for a year, no dodging calls or doors, picking a Yesponsor—then signed it three times and initialed twice, feeling the weight of it even as I joked, 'Is this like a legal document?'
Sanji pulled out a hot iron brand and pressed it into my palm—I yelled out—and then I saw 'YES' burned into my skin.
I stamped her loan form when Norman wasn't looking—five hundred bucks for a kid’s college books, off the books. Marge ratted me out again, but this time, I didn’t care.
I told that pawn guy I might have some stuff to pawn—didn’t even think about it, just said yes when he handed me the flyer.
I said I’d like to learn Korean, and then the Berlitz guy told me the class was starting right now—I didn’t say no, I just kept walking, but I remember that moment clearly.

I helped Renee load her giant harp into that old Volvo, and then she invited me to her 5 a.m. jogging and photo thing—five a.m., for sunrise shots. I said I guess I'll be doing that tomorrow, like it just slipped out, and now I actually have to get up that early.
I tried to lighten the mood with the Pizza Hat joke, and when Seb told me to eat my fish and fuck off, I just shoved the rest in my mouth and left—smiling, even—like it didn’t gut me.
I showed up to Renee's pre-dawn jog, exhausted and unprepared, and when she asked for my camera, I had to admit I forgot it and pulled out my phone instead.
The Arab guy reached for my phone, saw Renee’s picture, and said she was pretty. I pulled it back, asked how much he needed, and stamped the form when he said eighty-five hundred.
This little girl, maybe ten, sits there with her quiet mom, talking about selling lemonade—hundred cups in two days—and says she just needs three grand to expand. I stamped it without a word.
I remember sitting across from Norman, heart pounding, when he called me out about the microloans—I froze, then argued that helping people with small dreams is what banking should be about.

After Norman approved the pilot program and told me to keep it quiet, I zipped my lips and tossed the key—then later, Rooney showed up not needing a loan, just my help moving because it was cheaper than hiring help.
I raised my hand at the bank when Norman asked for someone to come up with a local marketing idea, and that’s how I ended up putting puppies in a box for 'Pet-a-Puppy' day.
I was in the language center classroom trying to say 'I like to drive with my mother' in Spanish when the door opened, and I remember doing that after already taking Korean too.

I looked down at the word 'Yes' on my palm, felt my throat tighten, and said it—just once, quietly—after Tony kissed me and asked if I wanted to go into his bedroom, even though I’d already said twice I had to leave.
I said I had herpes, and when I told him it was downstairs, he just asked if it was front door or back door like it was a joke—then told me to give it, and pushed me down.
I told Peter that if a guy asks me into his bedroom, I have to say yes — and then I admitted I actually hooked up with a dude, just to prove how committed I am to saying yes.
I left Peter's office with the kitten under my arm, heading to Korean class even though he reminded me I hate Korean food — but that doesn’t matter anymore.

Renee dumped more squid on my plate even after I said I was good, and then she admitted her art was terrible—her voice too high, her pottery like poo, her photos blurry—but she didn’t care, because not everything needs a goal. She said the world is a playground, like kids know but everyone forgets.

I caught myself saying the bank was lame out of habit, but then realized I actually like it now—especially the microloan program I started, helping people get small loans instead of going to loan sharks. I hadn’t noticed before how much I’ve started caring about it.

I was trying to play it cool, introducing myself normally, but then Khatoon asked if she knew me from PersianWifefinder.com and everything got quiet—I laughed because Renee did, but I wasn’t really laughing, I was just moving my face.
I said yes and pulled Renee in to kiss her—finally, something was going right—and we fell onto the bed, the boxes around us forgotten for a second.
I froze when I saw Rooney standing there—just watching—and I couldn't speak, didn't know how to react, and then Renee had to say no for me.
I kept massaging Renee even when my hands started cramping—she said 'don't stop,' and I just kept going, even though I could barely move my fingers.
She was asleep, murmuring 'please keep massaging,' and I did—kept going even though she wasn't awake to notice, my hands hurting bad.
I turned white when Chris Parker asked how I explained myself—my hands went cold, and all I could think was that I was about to get fired.
He actually shook my hand and invited me on a corporate golf trip—I said yes before I even realized what was happening.

I spent $1500 on dinner because the waiter asked if I wanted the expensive wine and Peter wasn’t there to stop me—I couldn’t say no, not when every 'yes' has led me this far. If I stop now, the whole thing might collapse.
She asked me in English, 'Kiss me? Please?' and I just said yes—nervously, like an idiot—before she pulled me into a passionate kiss.
After I pulled away and told her she was very sexy, we started kissing again, and I remember feeling guilty even as it was happening.
I walked into Chris's office with three drinks, and before I could even sit down, he offered me the VP role to expand the microloan program bankwide—I didn’t expect that, but I said yes right away.

I asked Sanji for help choosing between a job and traveling with a girl, and when he started pushing his overpriced seminar instead of answering, I realized he wasn't helping me—he was just selling something.
I started yelling in the coffee shop that Sanji was a con artist, my voice cracking, knowing everyone was staring, but I couldn't stop—I had this stupid yes burned into my hand because of him.
I typed back to that so-called King of Nigeria, calling him out—telling him he’s not a king, just some lying kid in Russia, and to never write me again or I’d find him and beat his face in.
I threw out all those stupid boxes of junk I’d bought online and took the six kittens to the ASPCA—felt like I was finally getting rid of the mess I’d let pile up.

dialogue_exemplars: I say yes. To everything. Say Yes More. It's that simple.
I've been a teller at Southwest Bank for ten years? How the hell did that happen? (doing the math) Ten years... if I had had a child, he'd be toilet-trained by now.

I am not a cave dweller. Just the other day, we all went to Summerfest and snuck backstage and you bet me I wouldn't steal something and so I stole a drumstick from that horrible Swedish hillbilly band. That's not very cave dweller of me.
What? So? I'm like a sexual camel. I only need it once every couple years.
Uch. Brunch coffee. Why can't they make it black without all this frothy shit?
I just love pets. This is Veronica, King George, Owen, Carl jr., Carl the III, Carl IV, Bubbles, Greedo, Cat 1, Cat 2 and Cat 3. At the end there, I got kind of bored of naming them.
You've slept on my couch for four weeks. You're a grown man. Now sack up and get the hell out of here.
Allow me to delete you, my liege.

relations.relation_summary: Carl Allen and Peter share a close, multifaceted relationship primarily defined by deep friendship and mutual support. Social relationship evidence consistently labels Peter as Carl's 'best friend' and highlights their frequent social interactions, including shared meals, celebrations, and personal conversations. Their emotional dynamic is characterized by trust and openness, as Carl confides in Peter about personal matters and Peter expresses concern about Carl's social withdrawal, even confronting him in an intervention-like moment when Carl misses events. A pivotal aspect of their bond is the formalization of an accountability structure when Carl appoints Peter as his 'Yesponsor,' mirroring Alcoholics Anonymous sponsorship, to support his commitment to saying 'yes' to new experiences. This role underscores Peter's influence on Carl's behavioral transformation. Key joint events reflect both camaraderie and tension: they engage in meaningful dialogue about marriage and life choices, eat together in Peter's office, and plan social gatherings like brunch and New Year's celebrations. However, their relationship also experiences strain, as seen when Carl physically pushes Peter out of his house in a moment of frustration, revealing underlying friction amid Carl's emotional resistance to change. Despite this, Peter extends an apology and reinvites Carl, who accepts, demonstrating resilience and emotional maturity in their bond. The relationship evolves from casual colleagues and friends into a more intentional, supportive partnership that directly impacts Carl's personal growth, encouraging him to re-engage with life and relationships. The combination of professional overlap and deep personal investment cements Peter as both a social anchor and a catalyst for Carl's transformation.

Carl Allen and Rooney share a multifaceted relationship defined by friendship, shared social indulgence, cooperation in physical tasks, and eventual conflict. Social relationship evidence consistently portrays them as friends who engage in casual, familiar interactions—Rooney jokes about getting Carl a beer, invites him to social events, and refers to their bond with nostalgic, childhood-like affection. Their friendship is reinforced through repeated joint participation in drinking activities, including doing jello shots and consuming beers at Senor Frogs, where they exhibit drunken camaraderie and mutual encouragement, such as during a karaoke contest. They also collaborate on practical tasks, most notably when Rooney asks Carl to help move a fridge, an event that results in Carl falling down the stairs—an incident that leads Carl to seek Rooney’s assistance despite Rooney’s own injury, indicating a level of trust and reliance. Their cooperative dynamic extends to playful rebellion, as seen when Rooney encourages Carl to throw a rock at Chris, suggesting alignment in impulsive behavior. However, the relationship deteriorates when Rooney overstays his welcome at Carl’s apartment, culminating in a confrontational conflict where Carl forcibly removes Rooney from the couch after a heated argument. This shift from camaraderie to hostility marks a clear evolution in their relationship, driven by boundary violations and mounting tension. The emotional dynamic moves from mutual enjoyment and support to frustration and antagonism, impacting Carl’s behavior by prompting him to assert personal boundaries, signaling a turning point in his character development. The evidence confirms both a strong social bond and a trajectory of deterioration rooted in shared experiences.

The relationship between Carl Allen and Sanji is defined by a mentor-mentee dynamic, where Sanji serves as a catalyst for Carl's personal transformation. Social relationship evidence shows a positive, respectful connection—Carl visits Sanji's hotel room to express gratitude for inspiration, indicating he views Sanji as a source of guidance. This is reinforced by their shared events: Sanji directly confronts Carl about his existential crisis, noting that life is passing him by, creating an emotionally charged moment of vulnerability. Carl responds while Sanji snaps emotionally, underscoring mutual awareness of time and regret, which deepens their connection. The pivotal event—Sanji branding Carl's palm with a 'YES'—symbolizes a ritualistic commitment to change, with Sanji enacting the transformation and Carl undergoing it. This act cements Sanji’s role as a mentor who imposes a new identity on Carl, directly influencing Carl’s subsequent behavior as he adopts the 'Yes Man' philosophy. The relationship evolves from a chance encounter to a defining influence on Carl’s decisions, rooted in emotional honesty and symbolic action. The evidence is insufficient to confirm long-term reciprocity or personal intimacy beyond this transformative phase.

The relationship between Carl Allen and Seung Kim is marked by emotional ambivalence, oscillating between moments of hostility and apparent friendship. Social relationship evidence reveals mutual accusations of sabotage, with Carl insulting Seung Kim as a 'son of a dog' and Seung Kim retaliating with professional undermining, indicating deep conflict and mistrust. These hostile exchanges suggest a breakdown in cooperation, possibly tied to tensions surrounding a business merger. However, in earlier interactions, there is evidence of affinity: Seung Kim speaks rapidly to Carl in a familiar manner, they share laughter, and he addresses Carl as 'my friend' in Korean, implying a prior bond or camaraderie. This contrast suggests a deteriorating relationship where personal friendship is strained by professional rivalry. The absence of common events prevents confirmation of shared experiences that might contextualize this shift. As a result, the emotional dynamics appear unstable, with no clear resolution or evolution confirmed in the evidence. The relationship's impact on character decisions is partially evident—Carl’s rejection of Seung Kim’s accusations culminates in him quitting, signaling a definitive break. However, the evidence is insufficient to confirm whether this rupture is permanent or if prior positive interactions had a lasting influence on their behaviors.

memories.memory_text: I remember asking Carl, 'You're going, already?' when he just up and left right after the ball drop—like none of us mattered enough to stick around for the damn song.
I called Carl to get him to come out—he was supposed to be part of this, all of us at Rudy’s—but he was already in bed at 11:15, like that was a real excuse.
I walked into Carl's apartment and called it an intervention because he missed our engagement party—again, he was just sitting there watching Hell's Kitchen like that was a real excuse.
I called Carl to apologize for barging in yesterday—told him it was his life to live, and he mumbled something like it was fine, barely awake.
I asked if he wanted to come to brunch with me, Lucy, and Kath, and after a weird pause, he said yes—sounded like he was being dragged into it, but he said it twice.
Carl shows up at brunch out of nowhere, and Kath says it's a surprise, which feels like everyone’s thinking it but no one wants to say it—except me, I just wonder why the hell he’s here.
I told Carl if he wanted to sit so bad, he should say something—next thing I know he’s arguing with the waitress about the seating list like it’s a goddamn courtroom.

I called out that Kath’s a fancy lawyer making bank — someone had to say it — and yeah, it was about time she started buying places instead of renting. She played it off, but come on, she’s doing better than all of us.
I told Carl the coffee was frothy because he ordered a latte—like that was somehow a mystery to him.
I ordered a normal-sized beer while Rooney went all out with the twenty-ouncers, and when Lucy and I laughed at Carl’s plea to not be left alone with Rooney, I didn’t even realize he was serious.
I shook hands with Carl after he called me his 'Yesponsor'—like this whole thing was some kind of recovery program—and I knew he wouldn’t last a week, but I played along.

Carl sat across from me eating a burger, totally calm, saying he had to say yes to everything—like giving loans to strangers or going into a guy’s bedroom and hooking up with him. I remember putting my burger down, the way my stomach turned when he said it like it was nothing.

He actually walked out with that damn kitten tucked under his arm, like the whole conversation hadn’t just gone off the rails. I just sat there, burger in hand, wondering when Carl stopped making decisions and started letting every random dude with a request make them for him.
I asked Carl if his suit was Hugo Boss, and when the conversation just stalled out, I said 'If you'll excuse me' and walked away.
I told Carl I was terrified about getting married—just blurted it out—and then worried whether not being able to tell ivory from cream made me a bad husband.

I was telling Carl to stick with what’s practical—keeping his job, his apartment—when my phone rang. I answered it mid-sentence, told my wife we should go with tulips instead of roses, then covered the phone to tell him I’d be a while and to go bother his guru.

I left Carl a message—joked about the engagement party and called him less gay, then invited him to Rudy’s. It was classic me: sarcastic, a little barbed, but really, I just wanted to see if he’d bite.
I was just standing there when the lights went out and Carl's voice boomed over the speakers announcing my engagement—like it was some kind of damn ceremony.
Then Carl rides in on a white horse, balloons falling, jumps off, and slaps a crown on my head—like this was normal, like a guy on a stallion belonged in a dive bar.
Carl shoved a set of keys into my hand and said I was supposed to sell all his stuff—like I’m some kind of liquidator for his life’s leftovers.

memories.memory_text: I handed Carl a flyer and asked if he wanted to rock out tonight, but he just said he doesn’t rock out and kept walking into Dunkin’ Donuts.

I held out that flier one more time, and for once, Carl didn’t just walk past—he actually stopped and took it. After a year and a half of ignoring me, he finally gave in, and I couldn’t help but smirk when he did.

I stuck out my hand and said, 'I'm Renee by the way,' and when he told me his name was Carl, I repeated it back—'Carl. Cool.'—like it was some kind of trophy. Felt good putting a name to the guy who finally caved after all my nonsense.
I told Carl to give back the extra flyer—he already had one, and they cost me money—but he just shrugged it off like it was no big deal.

I was talking to Carl after the show, trying to hit those super high notes for my water nymph song, and then he deadpans, 'I've known some water nymphs with big balls,' and I just—completely lose it. I start laughing like a maniac because it’s so weird and unexpected, and then he tosses out 'Big Balled Water Nymph' like it’s a real thing.

I was about to go up and help take down the gear when I joked to Carl, 'Unless of course, you want to help?'—totally just messing around—and then he actually says, 'Sure. I love clearing stages,' and jumps up. I was not expecting that at all.
I told Carl about my jogging photo group and invited him to come—five in the morning, sunrise shots, the whole deal. He seemed surprised, but I could tell he was intrigued.
I saw Carl show up looking like he hadn’t slept, and when he pulled out his phone instead of a real camera, I couldn’t help but tease him—‘Awesome idea. So light.’
As we jogged past that flower, I snapped a quick photo—just because it caught my eye, bright and there—and kept moving with the group.
I remember Carl snapping his phone away when that guy at the bank got too close to my picture—like it meant something just to him.

I remember pointing to that big brown plate that looked like poo and cracking myself up, then calling Carl out for showing up to every single one of my art shows—even the one way out in Fairfield County.
I remember the moment it clicked—he wasn’t creepy, he was just shy—and when he finally asked me out, I said yes and immediately suggested we do Korean, 'cause he mentioned taking Korean class.
I told Carl I already bought a ticket to go around the world in four months, and when he looked surprised, I admitted I was terrified—but saying it out loud made it feel real in the best way.
I walked in and these ten puppies and kittens came running at us—like, all at once—and I couldn’t help but blurt out, 'You work for the ASPCA?' because what the hell else do you say to that?
I looked at Carl and just asked him straight up, 'Well, are you going to make out with me or what?'—then he grabbed me and we were on the bed, and for a second, it was just us.

I heard someone speak and turned to see Rooney standing there—asked if he could watch, like it was normal. I didn’t hesitate: 'No, you can’t watch.' Didn’t ask Carl, didn’t second-guess. Just shut it down.
I remember asking Carl not to stop the massage after he paused the first couple times — I just wanted him to keep going, and I wasn’t done enjoying it.
I must’ve been really out of it, but I half-remember mumbling something about needing the massage to keep going, even after I’d fallen asleep — felt like a reflex.
Lucy mentioned we're having dinner tonight, though I didn't hear it directly from her or Carl.

I listed all the things I do—painting, band, ESL, shelter work, balloon animals—trying to show I’m more than just one thing, but then Carl cut in and reduced my pottery to 'really big,' like that was the only part worth mentioning.
I stopped kissing him because I could tell he wasn't really into it—he was too busy checking his damn watch.

I remember joking about sexy pottery, then actually meaning it when I suggested we just go to the airport and hop on the first flight—Carl said yes like he really wanted to, and that felt like something real.
I walked up and grabbed Carl's arm, then asked who that guy was—felt good to make my presence known right away.
I said 'It was nice meeting you' and walked off with Carl—polite, but I could feel the weirdness hanging in the air.
I remember giving Carl a flat 'It is?' when he got all excited about those old heavy headsets — ten and a half pounds, seriously? — and then cracking up when he shot back 'Not at all.'
I was still laughing when the old tour guide, dressed up like a 19th-century operator, suddenly goes full deadpan: 'This place is boring as shit' — I swear, I wasn't expecting that punchline at all.

I asked Carl if he’d want to travel around the world with me, then immediately backpedaled a little, saying I knew we hadn’t been seeing each other long—but I couldn’t hide that I was already falling.
After we kissed, I pulled back and joked about grabbing Nebraskan steaks before our flight—like we were already planning the next move of this thing that just started.

I was just walking off the plane with Carl when suddenly DEA agents swarmed us with barking dogs and screamed 'Get on the ground! Both of you!'—next thing I knew, they were kicking open the box and I was scrambling to stay out of the way.

They cracked open the chocolates and inside were tiny baggies of cocaine—white powder spilling out—and I remember thinking, 'No way this was just a gift,' but I didn’t say it out loud, just blurted, 'What the hell is that?'
I remember sitting there, realizing that every 'yes' he gave wasn’t because he agreed with me, but because he couldn’t help himself—he just defaulted to yes, like a broken machine.
When I asked if he was falling for me and he just said 'yes' again—same flat tone, no warmth—I felt it hit me: that answer didn’t mean anything, and it definitely wasn’t love.
I remember Carl saying he made a mistake letting me go—like it finally hit him what he’d lost, out of nowhere.
I remember turning around and seeing Carl there, asking him what he was doing here, and not even needing to wait for an answer—I just knew. Then I nodded, and we kissed.
Omar knelt and kissed my hand when we met, then told me to call him just 'Omar.'

I! Am! A! Fairy!/I! Like! To Fly!
A witches cauldron/burns hot as hell/As her crooked hand/Brews a love spell.

Watch your back, Carl. I mean it. I'm very litigious.
